---
title: "Self-check: Electron flow and mechanisms"
---

Answer each question before opening its explanation. Draw the relevant structure or step when asked; recognition alone can hide a charge or geometry error.

## 1. Where may a full-headed curved arrow start?

Choose a lone pair, an ordinary atom label without a specified electron pair, or a positive charge. Explain the electron accounting.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Check your answer"}
Start at a lone pair or a bond containing the pair being moved. A positive charge is an acceptor cue, not an electron-pair source.
:::

## 2. One arrow or two for carbonyl addition?

OH⁻ forms a new bond to carbonyl carbon. What must happen to the C=O π pair?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Check your answer"}
It moves to oxygen in the same addition step. Otherwise the carbon would have total bond order five. The original carbonyl oxygen becomes an alkoxide.
:::

## 3. Are two arrows two steps?

The methyl SN2 drawing has two curved arrows. Does it have two elementary steps?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Check your answer"}
No. Both pair movements occur in one concerted elementary step. Step counting depends on the mechanistic intermediates and barriers, not the number of arrows.
:::

## 4. What distinguishes an intermediate?

On a schematic free-energy profile, is an intermediate a maximum or a minimum? How does it differ from a transition state?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Check your answer"}
An intermediate is a minimum between elementary steps and has a finite lifetime. A transition state lies at a barrier maximum and is not an isolable species.
:::

## 5. What must a proton donor leave behind?

An alkoxide takes a proton from water. Give both products and check charge.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Check your answer"}
The products are an alcohol and OH⁻. Net charge starts and ends at minus one. Writing only alcohol would omit the donor-derived conjugate base.
:::

## 6. Does a catalyst favour products at equilibrium?

A catalyst lowers a kinetically relevant barrier. Does that change the equilibrium constant for the same reaction and conditions?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Check your answer"}
No. It changes the pathway and can speed approach to equilibrium in both directions. The same reactant/product endpoint free-energy difference determines the same equilibrium constant.
:::

If an answer was unexpected, return to the [worked practice](exercise.qmd), repair your own drawing and explain the change in a sentence.
